nameStory: Purple mullein gets its name from its stunning purple-pink flowers that set it apart from its more common yellow-flowered relatives. The name 'mullein' comes from the Latin 'mollis' meaning soft, referring to the fuzzy, velvety leaves that characterize this plant family. While most mulleins are yellow, this species breaks the mold with its vibrant purple blooms.
description: Purple mullein is a short-lived perennial that stands out in the mullein family with its eye-catching purple-pink flowers. This European native has naturalized in parts of New England, though it's quite rare here with only 8 recorded observations. The plant grows up to 3 feet tall or more, featuring a rosette of soft, fuzzy leaves at the base and a tall flowering spike that blooms earlier than other mullein species. It's hardy in our New England climate, thriving in USDA zones 4 to 8.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Vibrant purple to purple-pink flowers arranged in a tall, dense spike - this is the key feature that separates it from yellow-flowered mulleins. Each flower has five rounded petals and prominent stamens with fuzzy purple filaments.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, velvety leaves that feel like flannel to the touch, arranged in a basal rosette. The leaves are oval to lance-shaped and much less woolly than great mullein's thick, fuzzy foliage.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a low rosette of leaves in the first year, then sends up a single tall flowering stalk that can reach 3+ feet. The plant has a more delicate appearance than the robust great mullein.

idTips.label: Blooming Pattern
idTips.description: Blooms earlier in the season than other mullein species, typically starting in late spring to early summer. Flowers open from bottom to top along the spike over several weeks.

habitat: Purple mullein prefers well-drained, sandy or gravelly soils in full sun locations. Look for it in disturbed areas like roadsides, old fields, waste places, and rocky slopes. It's quite rare in New England, so finding one is a special treat for plant enthusiasts.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from the basal rosette, and flower stalks begin to develop. This is when you'll first notice the plant preparing to bloom earlier than other mulleins.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with the spectacular purple flower spike in full display. Seeds begin developing in small capsules after flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open to release tiny seeds. Leaves may begin to yellow and die back as the short-lived perennial completes its cycle.
seasonality.winter: Usually dies back completely, though some basal leaves may persist in milder winters. Seeds lie dormant in the soil waiting for spring germination.

funFact: Purple mullein is like the rebel of the mullein family - while nearly all other mulleins sport yellow flowers, this species boldly flaunts purple blooms, making it the 'purple sheep' of an otherwise yellow family!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other mullein species, but the purple flowers are a dead giveaway. All other common New England mulleins have yellow flowers, so if you see purple blooms on a plant with soft, fuzzy leaves and a tall flower spike, you've found the rare purple mullein.
contextualKnowledge: Purple mullein is extremely rare in New England with only 8 recorded observations, making it a prized find for botanists and plant enthusiasts. Don't be discouraged if you never see one - even experienced naturalists might go years without encountering this European escapee in our region.
compareHints: Purple mullein's vibrant purple flowers instantly separate it from great mullein's yellow blooms and much woolier leaves. Unlike moth mullein which has more widely-spaced yellow or white flowers, purple mullein has densely packed purple flowers. It's also generally smaller and more delicate than the robust great mullein, with less dramatically fuzzy foliage.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Great mullein is much larger and more robust than its relatives like moth mullein, which has a more branched, delicate appearance with less fuzzy leaves.
Among New England's mulleins, moth mullein stands out for its smooth leaves and scattered flower arrangement.
Orange mullein is distinguished from great mullein by its bright golden-orange flowers rather than pale yellow ones, and its leaves tend to clasp the stem more distinctly.
Among the mullein family in New England, dark mullein is unique for its combination of yellow flowers with dark purple stamens and multiple flowering stems.
Dense-flowered mullein differs from great mullein by having more tightly packed flowers with virtually no branching of the flower spike, while great mullein typically shows some small branches.
White mullein stands out from other mullein species by its loosely arranged flowers on individual stalks and its two-toned leaves that are much darker on top than underneath.
Among the mullein family, showy mullein stands out with its large branching flower clusters, while most other mulleins like great mullein have flowers arranged in simple spikes.
